hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever sat in a class or a conversation and felt completely lost?
options: then you’re in good company today. listen.
then you’ll like who’s sitting in the back. listen.
then imagine the greatest teacher of all, lost. listen.

steps.line: The Talmud tells this story. When Moses went up to receive the Torah, he found God tying tiny crowns onto the letters.
“Why the crowns?” Moses asked. God said: far in the future, a man named Akiva will draw heaps of teachings from every little stroke.
“Show me,” said Moses. And suddenly he was sitting in Rabbi Akiva’s classroom, at the very back, behind eight rows of students.

steps.q: Moses, who brought the Torah down the mountain, listens to Akiva’s class. How does he feel?
steps.why: He couldn’t follow it. The greatest teacher, lost in his own subject.

steps.line: He couldn’t follow what they were saying, and his strength drained away. Then a student asked, “Rabbi, how do you know this?”
Akiva answered, “It is a law given to Moses at Sinai.” And Moses, in the back row, was at peace.

steps.q: The Talmud doesn’t stop there. Moses asks God: you have a teacher like Akiva, and you give the Torah through me? What does God answer?
o: “Be silent. So it arose in My thought.”
steps.why: Menachot 29b. No neat reason, just “be silent.” The Talmud lets even Moses’s question stand open.

steps.q: Why is Moses comforted, even though he still doesn’t understand the class?
o: He realized his name was still famous
He saw he wasn’t needed anymore
The new teaching still grows from his
steps.why: Akiva’s teaching was new, but rooted in Sinai. The Torah keeps growing from the same source.

steps.line: Today, a Torah scroll is still written by hand, by a scribe called a sofer, on parchment, with a quill. Seven of the letters still get their tiny crowns.
steps.label: today

steps.q: A sofer must write every letter perfectly. If even one letter is missing or broken, what happens to the scroll?
o: It’s fine if the meaning is clear
It can’t be used until it’s fixed
It must be buried right away
steps.why: One missing or cracked letter makes a scroll unfit until a scribe repairs it. A scroll too damaged to fix is buried with care, like a person.

say: here’s what i love. torah isn’t just a book on a shelf. it’s the five books in the scroll, and the whole hebrew bible, and every good teaching since, down to a good answer at last night’s kitchen table.
and the scroll is read aloud, a section at a time, to the very end. then on simchat torah, the joy of the torah, the last line is read, and right away the first line again.

steps.q: If even Moses couldn’t follow Akiva’s class, what does the story say about learning Torah?
o: Being lost is part of learning it
Later teachers know more than Moses
steps.why: No one holds all of it. Even Moses sat in the back. Being lost is part of the learning.

today.say: find one verse or teaching you don’t understand. today, sit with it for a minute and ask one question: how do you know this? that’s how akiva’s students learned. look it up, ask someone, or just wonder.
options: that’s the eighth row. the best seat in the house.
good. reading is where the questions come from.

tomorrow.title: The day the scroll was read aloud.
tomorrow.line: a whole city stands in a square from dawn to noon, listening to one scroll. then they’re told to stop crying and go eat.

card.keepWhy: Every little stroke still has more to teach.
sources: Babylonian Talmud, Menachot 29b (Moses finds God tying crowns to the letters; a man named Akiva ben Yosef will expound heaps of laws on every tittle; ‘turn around’; Moses sits at the end of the eighth row and does not understand; his strength fails; ‘Rabbi, from where do you know this?’ ‘It is a law given to Moses at Sinai’; his mind is set at ease; the lesson paraphrases Moses’s question, which in the Talmud is ‘who is holding back Your hand?’, and leaves out the vision of Akiva’s death that follows)

Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Tefillin, Mezuzah and Torah Scroll (writing a Torah scroll); Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 36:3 (the crowns, tagin, on the seven letters shin, ayin, tet, nun, zayin, gimel, tsadi)
Deuteronomy 34:12 and Genesis 1:1 (the last and first lines read on Simchat Torah)
